objective_for_doctor: A 49-year-old Male patient presents to the clinic. Chief complaint: I have lower chest pain, upper chest pain, and right posterior chest wall radiating pain.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I have bad chest pain—lower and upper chest pain—and it feels like a knife-stab pain. It also goes to my right and left posterior chest wall and my thoracic spine, and I get significant shortness of breath with it, worse when I lie flat (orthopnea).

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—first, is the pain worse with deep breathing or pressing on your chest (tender to touch), and did it start suddenly or gradually?  
Doctor: Also, do you have fever, cough, recent infection, leg swelling, or any recent long travel/surgery?

Yes, it’s worse with deep breathing—very pleuritic. It started very suddenly, like an onset speed of 9/10. I don’t have fever or cough, and no recent infection, leg swelling, or recent long travel or surgery.

Doctor: Given sudden, very pleuritic “knife-stab” chest pain with shortness of breath and worse when lying flat, I’m concerned about a pulmonary or pleural cause—do you have any history of blood clots, smoking, or known heart/lung disease?  
Doctor: REQUEST TEST: ECG and Troponin; REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray; REQUEST TEST: CT_Pulmonary_Angiography (or V/Q scan if contrast not suitable).

I don’t know of any history of blood clots, and I don’t have smoking history or known lung disease that I’m aware of. I do have a past history of pericarditis, but I don’t have other known heart/lung problems.

Doctor: I’m going to check your vitals/exam—any oxygen saturation drop, fast heart rate, or do you feel faint when standing? Also, is the pain worse leaning forward (pericarditis-like) versus worse with specific chest wall movement or palpation?  
Doctor: REQUEST TEST: D-dimer and Repeat ECG (and consider Echocardiogram if ECG/Troponin suggest pericarditis).

I haven’t felt faint when standing, but I do feel very short of breath. The pain is worse with deep breathing, and it feels sharp/pleuritic; I’m not sure about leaning forward versus moving my chest or pressing on it.

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—can you check your current oxygen saturation if available, and how fast is your heart rate/blood pressure right now? Also, do you have any hemoptysis (coughing blood) or one-leg swelling?  
Doctor: REQUEST TEST: CT_Pulmonary_Angiography result review OR V/Q scan if CT not possible; REQUEST TEST: CBC and Basic Metabolic Panel (for safety/alternative causes).
I don’t have my oxygen saturation or my current heart rate/blood pressure numbers with me. I also don’t have coughing blood, and I don’t notice one-leg swelling.

Doctor: Based on what you’ve told me—sudden onset 9/10, sharp pleuritic pain worse with deep breath, and significant shortness of breath with orthopnea—I’m still most worried about a pulmonary embolism, though pericarditis/pleurisy and pneumothorax remain possible.  
Doctor: REQUEST TEST: STAT CT_Pulmonary_Angiography (or V/Q scan if contraindicated) + bedside lung ultrasound and chest X-ray now.  
Doctor: While those are pending, do you have any recent trauma to the chest or a history of connective-tissue disease (Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos), and is your pain strictly one-sided or truly bilateral?

No recent trauma to my chest. I don’t have any known connective-tissue disease like Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos. The pain is on both sides—I have right and left chest/breast and posterior chest wall pain, not strictly one-sided.

Doctor: Given the *sudden onset* and *severe pleuritic* bilateral chest pain with marked shortness of breath/orthopnea, the leading dangerous causes still are pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax; pleurisy/pericarditis are less classic for your “knife-stab” with orthopnea.  
Doctor: REQUEST TEST: STAT CT_Pulmonary_Angiography (or V/Q scan if CT can’t be done) and repeat Chest_X-Ray immediately; REQUEST TEST: Bedside_Echocardiogram to assess for pericardial effusion and right-heart strain.
Okay. I understand—please do the CT (or V/Q if needed) and the repeat chest X-ray and bedside echo. I’m still having the severe chest pain and shortness of breath, and it’s worse when I’m lying flat.

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—while we’re getting the CT/VQ, repeat chest X-ray, and bedside echo, one last safety check: do you have any new fainting, confusion, blue lips, or can you speak full sentences without gasping? Also, do you have any swelling/pain in one calf or have you been bedridden for more than 3 days recently?  
Doctor: If you can’t get those details right now, tell me: is the pain improving, worsening, or unchanged over the last hour?

I can speak full sentences without gasping, and I don’t have fainting, confusion, or blue lips. I don’t have swelling or pain in one calf, and I haven’t been bedridden for more than 3 days. Over the last hour the pain feels about the same—maybe slightly worse.

Doctor: I’m going to move you toward an emergency-workup diagnosis: given sudden severe pleuritic “knife-stab” pain, significant dyspnea/orthopnea, and no infectious symptoms, we still need to rule out pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax immediately—are your CT angiography and repeat chest X-ray/echo results back yet?  
Doctor: If those aren’t back, do you have an EKG/troponin and D-dimer result available right now, and what were your oxygen saturation and heart rate when you arrived?  
Doctor: DIAGNOSIS READY: Suspected Pulmonary Embolism (high-risk), pending CT pulmonary angiography/VQ and right-heart strain on echo

[DDX]
1. Pulmonary embolism
